title: Turning Interoperability into Impact: Connecting Data for Community Health
summary: For community health centers (CHCs), interoperability is becoming much more than an IT consideration. It is increasingly embedded in the infrastructure, reporting requirements, and quality improvement expectations that support value-based care.
body_markdown:
**Author: Adam Plotts, Vice President, Provider and Health System Solutions, Labcorp Diagnostics**


For community health centers (CHCs), interoperability is becoming much more than an IT consideration. It is increasingly embedded in the infrastructure, reporting requirements, and quality improvement expectations that support value-based care.


That shift is particularly relevant now.


The Health Resources and Services Administration’s (HRSA) current Health Center Controlled Network (HCCN) program, running from August 2025 through July 2028, identifies **Interoperability and data sharing as one of three required objectives** . The goal is to help participating health centers strengthen bidirectional information exchange to improve care coordination, reduce unnecessary testing and data duplication, make referral and information-sharing processes more effective, and reduce provider burden.


HRSA even identifies the use of Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) to automate clinical quality and other reporting as one way health centers can advance interoperability.


At the same time, HRSA is modernizing Uniform Data System reporting through UDS+. Health centers will be required to submit a minimum amount of de-identified, patient-level UDS+ data each year using HL7 FHIR standards.


Together, these initiatives point toward a future in which better connected data isn't separate from quality improvement. Rather, it helps make quality improvement possible.


## What connected data can mean at the point of care


The value of interoperability for CHCs becomes much more tangible when viewed through the[experience of Health Services of North Texas (HSNT)](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/videos/data-made-difference-how-routine-visit-revealed-critical-care-gap) .


HSNT has been on a broader journey to improve quality performance and close gaps in care across the communities it serves.[Since implementing Labcorp Diagnostic Assistant®](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/case-studies/closing-gaps-lab-data-strengthen-clinical-decisions) , the organization has incorporated more connected diagnostic information into clinical workflows, helping providers access longitudinal Labcorp data directly within their existing EHR experience.


That access can make an important difference.


In one example, a provider reviewing a patient's information through Diagnostic Assistant discovered a previous abnormal cervical cancer screening result that required follow-up. The previous Labcorp screening test had been ordered by another clinic but the results were available to the HSNT care team through Diagnostic Assistant during the patient encounter. Instead of relying on disconnected records or spending days or weeks trying to locate the information, the provider was able to act while the patient was there.


Follow-up was initiated, with the patient actively participating in the next steps.


It is a powerful example of what interoperability is ultimately intended to accomplish: not simply moving data between systems but making the right information available when and where it can help inform care.


It also brings to life one of the outcomes HRSA specifically associates with greater interoperability: reducing unnecessary medical testing and data duplication. When existing diagnostic information is accessible within the clinical workflow, providers may have greater visibility into what has already been performed before deciding what needs to happen next.


## Supporting a broader quality-improvement journey


For HSNT, connected diagnostic information is part of a broader focus on improving quality and proactively identifying gaps in care.


The organization has advanced from **Bronze to Silver HRSA recognition** while continuing to strengthen its approach to quality improvement. Diagnostic Assistant helps support that work by making longitudinal Labcorp information easier for clinicians to access and use within their workflow.


It can also make preparation more efficient. Instead of searching across systems and sources for available laboratory history, care teams can access relevant Labcorp information within the EHR workflow, helping them identify overdue testing, screenings, and follow-up needs before or during the patient encounter.


> As Karishma Patel, Physician’s Assistant and Clinical Informatics Lead at HSNT has described the shift, **“When data is available during the visit, care becomes proactive, not reactive.”**


For organizations managing large patient populations, limited resources, and growing quality expectations, that distinction matters.


## Bringing interoperability into the clinical workflow


Diagnostic Assistant is designed to complement, not replace, the EHR.


Using standards-based interoperability, including SMART on FHIR technology, Diagnostic Assistant brings Labcorp diagnostic information and capabilities into the provider's existing EHR workflow. This gives care teams access to longitudinal Labcorp information without requiring them to leave their primary clinical environment to search for it.


For CHCs, that model aligns with a broader direction across healthcare: moving away from fragmented information and disconnected workflows toward more interoperable, digitally enabled care.


HRSA's HCCN priorities reinforce that direction. Along with interoperability and UDS+ implementation, the program identifies data management and analytics as a required objective and value-based care as an elective objective. HRSA specifically describes health IT and the better use of data as tools that can help health centers improve clinical quality, health outcomes, care coordination, and the patient and provider experience.


## From exchanging data to using it


FHIR and interoperability standards provide important infrastructure. But the greater opportunity is what community health centers can do when that infrastructure makes useful information available within everyday clinical workflows.


For CHCs, that can mean giving providers greater visibility into a patient's diagnostic history, identifying care gaps earlier, reducing unnecessary duplication, simplifying chart preparation, and supporting more informed decisions at the point of care.


It can also help create the digital foundation for a healthcare environment increasingly focused on standardized data exchange, digital quality reporting, and value-based outcomes.


HSNT's experience demonstrates the practical side of that transformation. When diagnostic information becomes easier to access and act upon, interoperability moves from a technology concept to something much more meaningful: **a solution for helping care teams turn connected data into better-informed care.**
